## QUESTION 1

<!-- Make sure at least one of your charts includes reference marks!! -->

__Make a new column that represents the total number of babies with your name for only those states in which you have lived. (If you have only ever lived in one state, pick at least one other state so you get practice summing across columns). Make a graph displaying that total for your name over time.__

Just like the last assignment, 1960 is the most popular year for my name. I have lived in Texas, Utah, and Idaho.

```{python}
# Q1

my_name = "Jay"
my_states = ["TX", "UT","ID"]

my_name_states = (
    df
    .filter(pl.col("name") == my_name)
    .with_columns(
        pl.sum_horizontal(my_states).alias("my_states_total")
    )
    .select(["name", "year", *my_states, "my_states_total"])
    .sort("year")
)

max_point = (
    my_name_states
    .sort("my_states_total", descending=True)
    .head(1)
)

(
    ggplot(my_name_states, aes(x="year", y="my_states_total"))
    + geom_line()
    + geom_point(data=max_point, mapping=aes(x="year", y="my_states_total"), size=4)
    + geom_text(
        data=max_point,
        mapping=aes(x="year", y="my_states_total", label="my_states_total"),
        nudge_y=5,
        format="d"
    )
    + labs(
        title=f"Use of the Name {my_name} in Selected States",
        subtitle=f"States included: {', '.join(my_states)}",
        x="Year",
        y=f"Babies Named {my_name}"
    )
    + scale_x_continuous(format=".0f")
)

```


## QUESTION 2

1. __Let's look at a name that is special for members of the church: Brigham. For each year, calculate what proportion of babies named Brigham were born in Idaho and Utah? Make a graph displaying the proportion over time.__  

It looks like up until the 90s it was only Idaho and Utah that had Brigham, but it started to be used in other states after that.

```{python}
# Q2

brigham_proportion = (
    df
    .filter(pl.col("name") == "Brigham")
    .filter(pl.col("Total") > 0)
    .with_columns(
        ((pl.col("ID") + pl.col("UT")) / pl.col("Total")).alias("id_ut_proportion")
    )
    .select(["name", "year", "ID", "UT", "Total", "id_ut_proportion"])
    .sort("year")
)

(
    ggplot(brigham_proportion, aes(x="year", y="id_ut_proportion"))
    + geom_line()
    + labs(
        title="Proportion of Babies Named Brigham Born in Idaho and Utah",
        x="Year",
        y="Proportion Born in ID or UT"
    )
    + scale_x_continuous(format=".0f")
    + scale_y_continuous(format=".0%")
)

```

## QUESTION 3

1. __Consider doing some data validation. For the name David, calculate a sum of all 50 states and District of Columbia for each year. Now compare that total to the value in the 'Total' column. In which years, if any, do they not agree?__

This table shows all the years where the sum of all the states doesn't match the total column for David. It is empty, which means that in all the years, they agree. 

```{python}
# Q3

state_columns = [col for col in df.columns if col not in ["name", "year", "Total"]]

david_validation = (
    df
    .filter(pl.col("name") == "David")
    .with_columns(
        pl.sum_horizontal(state_columns).alias("state_sum")
    )
    .with_columns(
        (pl.col("state_sum") - pl.col("Total")).alias("difference")
    )
    .filter(pl.col("difference") != 0)
    .select(["name", "year", "state_sum", "Total", "difference"])
    .sort("year")
)

david_validation

```
